newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Dispute over envoys reflects deep split in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Dispute over envoys reflects deep split in Bosnia.

text.p: Rival political leaders in Bosnia cannot agree on how to divide up ambassadorial posts for the same reason they cannot agree on the nature of their peacetime state, diplomats said on Tuesday.
Western countries suspended contacts with Bosnian envoys this week after politicians failed to reach agreement on the distribution of diplomatic posts by an August 1 deadline imposed by major powers.
At the heart of the dispute is the wartime nationalism which guides the three Moslem, Croat and Serb political parties still dominating the country.

Bosnia's current ambassadors were appointed during the 1992-95 war by the Moslem-led government which fought for independence against Serb separatists and, at one point, against the Croats, their nominal allies.
Serb and Croat nationalists have long accused the Moslems, which form the largest ethnic community in Bosnia, of trying to dominate the central government and the diplomatic service.

Serb and Croat nationalists, ignoring the terms of a peace treaty, distrust the idea of Bosnian statehood and have preferred to view the territory under their control as extensions of neighbouring Croatia or Serbian-led Yugoslavia.

For the wartime Moslem-dominated government, retaining control over the ambassadorial posts was crucial to securing international support during the war and for legitimising the republic's break from old Yugoslavia.
The diplomatic freeze announced by European countries and the United States is largely symbolic but it has deeply angered the Moslems who feel they are being singled out for punishment.
Rival leaders have argued for months about how to divide up the 33 ambassadorial jobs around the world, including the coveted Washington posting, and what policy the envoys should promulgate.

Mediators in the office of the High Representative to Bosnia proposed distributing the most important posts equally among the three sides and the remainder based on the size of Moslem, Croat and Serb populations.
But the proposal collapsed over who would control the Washington posting.

The Moslems, seeking to retain the current ambassador in Washington who is a Bosnian Jew, called for some posts to be distributed to the eight percent of the population which falls outside the three communities.
"The proposal from the office of the High Representative ignores the rights of minorities," said Mirza Hajric, an aide to the Moslem chairman of the collective presidency, Alija Izetbegovic.

Even if the three sides agree on the distribution of posts, representatives of Bosnia's Serb entity have refused to agree to any joint foreign policy statement that would define common ground for envoys from the former warring factions.
The Serbs even oppose housing the foreign ministry in a single building and have lobbied for separate buildings, one in Moslem-Croat federation territory and one in the Serb entity.
The former High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, has said that appointing new ambassadors would reassure Croats and Serbs that the Moslems were willing to share power in peacetime.
But some Western officials sympathised with the U.S. view that the diplomatic freeze hurt the Moslem leadership, which they say has been more willing to cooperate with peacemakers.
"They are punishing the Moslems for what is essentially Serb recalcitrance," said one official.
A spokesman for the current High Representative, Carlos Westendorp, said there was only so much Western powers could do to persuade nationalist leaders to make their fragile state function.

"This is not a protectorate and it's not up to the international community to tell these people how to run their own country...," Simon Haselock, a spokesman for Westendorp, told reporters. "They are being given the opportunity and they must grasp it."
